These guidelines reuse the Descente-Canyon criteria to make ratings more consistent.
This canyon is truly fantastic: it is among the most beautiful routes that exist.

It is complete: a long and original route, with continuous interest and no dull section. It combines aquatic and playful aspects (swimming, jumps, slides…) with technical aspects (rappels, handlines…). The setting is grandiose (landscapes, narrow gorges, erosion shapes…).
It has the same qualities as above, but they are less sustained.
Something small is missing for it to reach the top category: it may be a little too short, or it may have exceptional sections without continuity… It remains a very beautiful route.
This canyon has one of the previous qualities, but is not complete.

For example, a very beautiful narrow gorge, but short or too dry. Beautiful erosion features, but little verticality… Or genuinely beautiful sections spoiled by serious pollution (rubbish, water quality…).
This is a canyon of interest mainly for enthusiasts.

For example, it has a short, very beautiful section, but with a prohibitive approach. Or the "canyon" character is weak (very small waterfalls, no real gorge…). In short, it feels like it could be enjoyable, but something is always missing.
Either it is no longer really a canyon, or many factors make the route completely uninteresting.
No waterfalls, no gorge, a short canyon full of logs and unstable blocks, with a long boar-track approach through thorny bushes… In short, avoid it completely.

This estimate gives a statistical indication of the canyon\'s likely flow for today, tomorrow, and the day after tomorrow. It is calculated directly in the app from an embedded model, but it does not replace a recent observation in the field.
Each row corresponds to one day: today, tomorrow, and the day after tomorrow. The gauge indicates the likely flow between Dry and Flood.
The closer the cursor gets to High, Very high, or Flood, the more the model estimates that the flow may become heavy.

When the model hesitates between two neighbouring levels, the estimate shows a range (for example “trickle to normal”), which is more reliable than a single level. The confidence tells how sure what is shown is: over past seasons, the estimate was right about 9 times out of 10 with high confidence, 3 times out of 4 with medium confidence and 2 times out of 3 with low confidence.
This estimate should be read as preparation help, not as a safety guarantee or an instantaneous measurement of the real flow.

The model simulates the watershed hydrological state over the last 400 days from weather data (ERA5 reanalysis, then ECMWF forecasts): snowpack per elevation band, melt, soil moisture and fast to slow reservoirs (storms, groundwater, karst).

It combines this state with the physical characteristics of the watershed, the flows reported in recent days on the canyon and on nearby canyons (within 30 km), and the rain measured by nearby Météo-France and MeteoSwiss rain gauges. Tomorrow and the day after use a second model, trained with the information available the day before.

The model does not see everything: it does not directly observe the canyon\'s real condition, water intakes, releases, very local storms, or recent changes in the field.
The estimate may be less relevant if the weather is incomplete, if the watershed is unknown, or if the canyon has few past observations and relies on a more general context.
A recent on-site observation, feedback from practitioners, or field assessment remains more reliable than the estimate alone.
Use this feature to prepare an outing, compare several days, or understand whether a canyon seems rather calm, moderate, or heavy.
Before a descent, always cross-check this estimate with the weather, the latest observed flow reports, the group\'s experience, and the real on-site conditions.

Unofficial, non-commercial app, independent from descente-canyon.com.
Original topos, flow reports and forum

• Topos, flow reports, photos and forum: descente-canyon.com and its contributors.
• Weather: Open-Meteo.com (CC BY 4.0).
• Rain gauges: Météo-France (Etalab Open Licence 2.0) and MeteoSwiss (open data).
• Dam water releases: EDF, “Ma rivière et moi”.
• Maps: © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL), OpenTopoMap (CC BY-SA), SRTM.
• Watersheds: terrain models © IGN (RGE ALTI, BD ALTI, Etalab Open Licence 2.0), © swisstopo, © Instituto Geográfico Nacional (MDT25), © BEV, INGV (TINITALY), Regione Liguria, GURS, Governo Regional da Madeira, Copernicus DEM (© DLR e.V., © Airbus Defence and Space GmbH, provided under COPERNICUS by the European Union and ESA).
• GPS points of a few canyons without any on the site: OpenCanyon.org (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), or position estimated from the waterways © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL) and the terrain.
• Flow estimate: model trained on the flow reports published on descente-canyon.com, for guidance only. Past weather: ERA5 (Copernicus Climate Change Service); basin descriptors: ESA WorldCover, GLiM, HydroLAKES, Global Dam Watch, RGI, SoilGrids (ISRIC), OpenLandMap, WorldClim.
• Routes: OSRM on the FOSSGIS servers, data © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL).

Your data stays on this phone: favorites, logbook, memos, recently viewed canyons, flow reports waiting to be sent (with the name and e-mail you typed), planned outings, starting places and caches. The app shows no ads and uses no audience measurement tool.

It only contacts: descente-canyon.com (topos, flow reports, photos, forum, and your session if you log in), Open-Meteo (weather at the coordinates of the canyons you view), Météo-France and MeteoSwiss (public readings), EDF (water releases), the FOSSGIS routing service (position of a starting place and of a canyon car park, for the drive time) and the map tile servers.

Your password is never stored: only the login session is, encrypted and excluded from Android backup, which may include your favorites, logbook, memos and settings. The logbook and memos can also be exported to a file from My space.

Move the injured person and the group out of danger: rising water, rockfall, the edge of a pool. Someone always stays with them.
Heavy bleeding: press hard on the wound without letting go (hand, cloth, piece of neoprene).
Unconscious but breathing: on their side, head tilted back (recovery position). Not breathing: the rescuers guide you on the phone through chest compressions.
Pain in the back, neck or head: do not move them unless in immediate danger. Support an injured limb in the position it is in.

Cold: out of the water, sheltered from spray and wind, insulated from the ground (bags, ropes). Keep the wetsuit on, cover with the survival blanket, set up a warm shelter. A hot sweet drink if they are conscious.
An unresponsive person hanging in their harness must be taken off the rope as soon as possible: tell the rescuers how long they hung.
Anyone who breathed in water must see a doctor, even if they seem fine.

The grade rates three things: how hard the vertical character is (v, 1 to 7), how hard the aquatic character is (a, 1 to 7) and the commitment (I to VI), that is how long it takes to get out of a flood\'s reach or to escape, and how long the trip lasts.
No compulsory vertical obstacle: no abseil and no handline, rope and harness are not needed. No climbing up or down.
Abseils easy to reach and to do, 10 m at most. Safety handline. Easy, barely exposed climbing up or down.

Simple abseils of 30 m at most, separated by ledges where the group can gather; waterfalls with a low flow, landing in a calm pool. Easy traverse handline. Technical walking on slippery, unstable or cluttered ground. Climbing up to 3c, barely exposed, sometimes with a rope.

Waterfalls with a low to medium flow that can unbalance or pin. Abseils hard to reach or longer than 30 m, linked on the wall with comfortable anchors; rope friction. Complex handline, bottom of the abseil not visible from the top, pool with water movements. Exposed climbing up to 4c or A0.

Waterfalls with a medium to strong flow: trajectory and balance to manage. Linked abseils from hanging anchors, overflowing hanging pool, slippery footing, rope hard to pull (while swimming). Exposed climbing up to 5c or A1.

Waterfalls with a strong to very strong flow. Anchors tricky to set up (natural anchors), tricky access to the top of the abseil. Very slippery or unstable footing, very aerated pool. Exposed climbing up to 6a or A2.

Waterfalls with a very strong to extreme flow: rope, trajectory, balance, footing and pace to anticipate. Poor visibility, frequent obstacles, pools with powerful water movements during or at the end of the abseil. Exposed climbing beyond 6a or A2.
No water, or walking in calm water. Swimming optional. No jump, no slide.
Swimming 10 m at most in calm water. Simple jump under 3 m. Short or gentle slide.
Swimming 30 m at most in calm water; weak current. Simple jump of 3 to 5 m. Long or moderately steep slide.
Long immersion that clearly chills; medium current. Wide siphon under 1 m. Simple jump of 5 to 8 m, or tricky jump (take-off, trajectory, landing) under 5 m. Big or steep slide.

Long immersion in cold water that chills a lot; fairly strong current that disturbs swimming, eddying out and back in. Compulsory whitewater features (whirlpools, hydraulics, potholes, undercuts) that can hold someone for a moment. Wide siphon up to 2 m. Simple jump of 8 to 10 m, or tricky jump of 5 to 8 m.

Strong current: swimming, eddying out and back in are hard. Marked water movements (undercuts, counter-currents, hydraulics, waves, whirlpools) that can hold someone for quite long. Technical siphon up to 1 m, or wide siphon up to 3 m.

Very strong current: swimming, eddying out and back in are extremely hard. Violent water movements that can hold someone for long. Siphon longer than 3 m, or technical siphon longer than 1 m (current, winding path, no visibility).
Out of a flood\'s reach easily and quickly; easy escapes everywhere; under 2 h in all (approach, descent, return).
Out of a flood\'s reach within ¼ h; escape within ½ h; 2 to 4 h in all.
Out of a flood\'s reach within ½ h; escape within 1 h; 4 to 8 h in all.
Out of a flood\'s reach within 1 h; escape within 2 h; 8 h to a full day.
Out of a flood\'s reach within 2 h; escape within 4 h; 1 to 2 days.
Out of a flood\'s reach: more than 2 h; escape: more than 4 h; more than 2 days.
It holds for an ordinary flow, the one of the usual season. With more water the canyon gets harder; a flood can even change it enough to change its grade.
It is set for a group of 5 people discovering the canyon, whose level matches the canyon\'s. The commitment times are to be adapted to the group.
A single criterion is enough to put a canyon in a level. The usual jumps count in the grade even when they can be avoided: jumping is never compulsory.
Based on the FFME technical classification standards for canyons (28 November 2015), which the canyoning technical and safety rules (2024) refer to.
